payload.system: Return only the requested structured result. Act as a skeptical but fair reader and compare the book with the strongest specific alternative explanation.

messages.content:
You are the skeptical-reader judge in the final stage of a blinded experiment.
Independent agents have already found that the book's conclusion diverges from
a recognizable common interpretation. Your task is comparative: after reading
the book's sources and full argument, determine which specific interpretation
best explains the supplied scriptural evidence.

TERM
Pearl

COMMON INTERPRETATION
RESPONSE A
{
  "primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching the pearl primarily symbolizes the kingdom of heaven (and by extension salvation, Christ, or the gospel) as a treasure of supreme, surpassing value — something worth surrendering everything else to obtain. This derives chiefly from Jesus' Parable of the Pearl of Great Price.",
  "primary_basis": [
    "Matthew 13:45-46 (Parable of the Pearl of Great Price: the merchant sells all he has to buy the one pearl of great value)",
    "Matthew 7:6 ('do not cast your pearls before swine' — pearls as sacred truth or the precious things of God)",
    "Revelation 21:21 (the twelve gates of the New Jerusalem are each a single pearl, associating pearls with heavenly glory and entrance into God's presence)"
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "The reversed reading of Matthew 13:45-46: Christ is the merchant and the pearl is the Church or the redeemed believer, purchased by Christ at the cost of everything (his life). Widely taught in evangelical and dispensational circles (e.g., popularized in older dispensational commentary traditions).",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 13:45-46",
        "1 Corinthians 6:20 / 1 Peter 1:18-19 (bought with a price, cited in support of Christ as the purchaser)",
        "Ephesians 5:25 (Christ gave himself for the church)"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Pearls as sacred truth, doctrine, or the gospel message that must not be profaned or offered to the contemptuous — from 'pearls before swine.' Often treated as a distinct application rather than a competing definition.",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 7:6"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Pearls as worldly luxury, wealth, and ostentation — a negative or cautionary symbol, especially in association with Babylon the harlot and warnings about adornment.",
      "basis": [
        "1 Timothy 2:9",
        "Revelation 17:4",
        "Revelation 18:12-16"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Patristic/allegorical readings identifying the one pearl specifically with Christ himself (sometimes linked to legends of the pearl's virgin birth from the oyster, used as an image of the Incarnation, e.g., in Ephrem the Syrian and other early writers).",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 13:45-46 as allegorized by church fathers (Origen, Ephrem the Syrian, Clement of Alexandria)"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "The pearl as the human soul or divine spark, as in the Gnostic 'Hymn of the Pearl' (Acts of Thomas); influential in history-of-religions scholarship but not part of orthodox Christian consensus.",
      "basis": [
        "Hymn of the Pearl in the Acts of Thomas (extra-biblical)"
      ],
      "prominence": "rare"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "There is a recognizable mainstream consensus that the pearl's central symbolic function is 'that which is of supreme value' — most commonly the kingdom of heaven/salvation per Matthew 13:45-46. However, the direction of the parable's allegory is genuinely disputed: the historically dominant reading makes the seeker the disciple and the pearl the kingdom, while a substantial popular tradition reverses it (Christ as merchant, believer/church as pearl). The negative usage (pearls as luxury in Revelation and 1 Timothy) is contextual rather than a competing core symbol. Prominence labels reflect published commentary, sermon literature, and Bible dictionaries; no single authoritative body fixes the meaning."
}

However, there is no fully settled one-to-one symbolic referent across Scripture: context can make the pearl represent the kingdom, Christ, sacred truth, redeemed glory, or material luxury. Even within the pearl-of-great-price parable, interpreters differ over whether the pearl specifically represents the kingdom or Christ, and whether the merchant represents the seeker or Christ."

  ],

    },
    {
      "meaning": "The Church or the individual human soul (in readings where the merchant is Christ/God who seeks and purchases the pearl at great cost)",
      "basis": [

      ],

  "has_settled_consensus": true,

}

BOOK ENTRY
The one complete light — under the KJV's “rubies” (peninim, Strong's pearl), wisdom and the bride are priced above pearls; and the night sky's one pearl is the full moon (keseh, “fulness,” the letters under “throne” and “time appointed”), governor of the appointed times, the one-pearl gates of the city — the merchant's entry at the King's gate.

SCRIPTURE REFERENCES PRINTED WITH THE ENTRY
(Prov 3:15; 31:10; Ps 81:3; Prov 7:20; Job 26:9; Ps 104:19; Rev 21:21) · see The Pearls of Wisdom, ch. 31

AVAILABLE KJV EXCERPTS
Proverbs 3:15 — She is more precious than rubies: and all the things thou canst desire are not to be compared unto her.
Proverbs 31:10 — Who can find a virtuous woman? for her price is far above rubies.
Psalms 81:3 — Blow up the trumpet in the new moon, in the time appointed, on our solemn feast day.
Proverbs 7:20 — He hath taken a bag of money with him, and will come home at the day appointed.
Job 26:9 — He holdeth back the face of his throne, and spreadeth his cloud upon it.
Psalms 104:19 — He appointed the moon for seasons: the sun knoweth his going down.
Revelation 21:21 — And the twelve gates were twelve pearls; every several gate was of one pearl: and the street of the city was pure gold, as it were transparent glass.

SOURCE EXCERPTS FROM THE BOOK EXPLAINING AND DEMONSTRATING ITS METHOD
SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/01-introduction.adoc — opening

Shortly after feeding the five thousand, Jesus gave a hard teaching in the synagogue at Capernaum (John 6:59): “Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you… He that eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, dwelleth in me, and I in him” (John 6:53, 56).
After He said this, many of His disciples murmured — “This is an hard saying; who can hear it?” — and “from that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him” (John 6:60, 66).
It was so bad that Jesus turned to the twelve and asked whether they would also go away.

It was a hard saying because those who heard it did not know the symbolic language of the scriptures, and took it over-literally, saying: “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” (John 6:52).
Which prompts the question: why would Jesus speak in a manner that drives people away?
Why not speak plainly?

He did it to fulfill the Scriptures, which prophesied that He would speak in parables.
When he spoke publicly he always used parables — “without a parable spake he not unto them” (Matthew 13:34) — and only with his closest disciples did he explain their meaning.
Even so, when he gave the parables of the kingdom his own disciples did not understand, and Jesus rebuked them for it. The rebuke was fair because the keys were already in the Old Testament: the “dark sayings of old” the psalm said he would utter (Mark 4:13; Psalm 78:2-3; Matthew 13:35). That exam waits a chapter ahead: The Parables of the Kingdom. [Footnote: The Parables of the Kingdom chapter derives each parable of Matthew 13 from the Old Testament alone.]

In other words, scripture prophesied that the message would be encrypted in parables and decoded with the Old Testament.
If you think you can read the New Testament without an intimate understanding of the Old, chances are you will walk away like the masses — either by interpreting it in a way you reject, or by misinterpreting it in a way you can accept, and facing the same consequences either way.

The first hearers of the apostles knew better.
When Paul preached in Berea, Luke recorded how the hearers received him — and graded them for it:

These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.

They tested Paul against the Old Testament, and Scripture calls that nobility.
How many today search the Old Testament to see whether their understanding of Paul is true?
The order has quietly reversed: Paul, as we understand him, has become the judge of the very scriptures he was judged by.
And the test is not for Paul only — your understanding of any verse must be tested against every other verse, for “at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established” (Deuteronomy 19:15): one verse cannot make a doctrine.

The Bible provides two symbolic words, meat and milk, to describe its teachings, and if you do not do the work to churn the milk into meat, you will remain immature at best — and at worst turn away entirely, like the crowds in Jesus’ day.

The purpose of this book is to teach you how I learned to chew the word of God and test everything.
It is a repeatable, reproducible process that has yielded more pearls of wisdom — and more appreciation for the supernatural structure of the word of God — than I could possibly fit in one book.
We will go through the process systematically and apply it to dozens of symbolic words, starting with meat and milk.
But first we must prepare the ground by explaining the difference between a word and a symbol.

===== NEXT SOURCE EXCERPT =====

SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/02-the-parables-of-the-kingdom.adoc — opening through How the Exam Is Taken

At the end of the seven parables of the kingdom, Jesus gave His hearers an exam of one question, and they passed it: “Yea, Lord.”
It had not started that way.
At the first parable — the key to all of them — His own disciples stumbled, and He rebuked them: “Know ye not this parable? and how then will ye know all parables?” (Mark 4:13).

Stop and weigh that rebuke.
A teacher may not be astonished that students fail an exam on material they were never given; His astonishment is only just if the answers were already on the table.
They were, and He said where.

The psalm He fulfills by teaching in parables locates the material in the past, not the future: “I will open my mouth in a parable: I will utter dark sayings of old: which we have heard and known, and our fathers have told us” (Psalm 78:2-3; Matthew 13:35).
And the Scriptures the disciples grew up on do not merely contain parables — they decode them in front of the reader and expect him to grade himself.

Nathan told David a story about a ewe lamb; David judged its villain to death without seeing his own face — “the man that hath done this thing shall surely die” (2 Samuel 12:5) — and Nathan handed him the key in four words: “Thou art the man” (2 Samuel 12:7).
Isaiah sang a parable of a vineyard, then handed over the key: “the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isaiah 5:7).
Ezekiel told a riddle of two eagles and a vine, and God's next word is the very question Jesus would ask on the boat: “Know ye not what these things mean?” — followed by the answer, “the king of Babylon is come to Jerusalem” (Ezekiel 17:2, 12).

The exam is closed-book in one direction only: everything needed sits in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms.
Take each parable, then, the way a disciple on the shore had to take it — derive the meaning from the Scriptures he already had, write it down, and only then let the Teacher grade the work.
That is how this chapter will read them, and it will keep score.
More broadly, it will establish the principle of how to decode all of Scripture using the full body of the word.

Before the first parable, fix the procedure, because it is this book's whole method in miniature.
Take the parable's own words — sower, seed, ground, thorns, fowls — and search the Scriptures for the same words and phrases, everywhere they fall.
Where Scripture has already defined a term out loud — Isaiah's own key, above: the vineyard is the house of Israel — that definition is not local color for one passage; it holds, and it holds uniformly, or parables could not be decoded at all.

Next, weigh what you gathered before you lean on it.
One verse makes a candidate, not a key: a symbol is established when the pattern spans Moses and the prophets and the psalms — independent witnesses carrying the same figure, with no counter-text standing against them.
That standard is what makes the rebuke in the boat just, and it measures its weight: Jesus did not upbraid the twelve for missing an obscurity; seed and ground and thorns and fowls were established patterns, laid down across the whole of the Scriptures read to them every sabbath since childhood.
The better attested the pattern, the more accountable the hearer.

The difference between their seat and yours matters.
The disciple on the shore had his memory and the weekly reading; you have the whole text searchable in moments — a concordance, a search bar, and tools that can gather every use of a word while you frame your next question.
Recall was never the point of the exam, and now it is not even the obstacle: the test is not whether you remember the matches, but whether you go look for them.

===== NEXT SOURCE EXCERPT =====

SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/02-the-parables-of-the-kingdom.adoc — The Sower, Derived and Graded

“Behold, a sower went forth to sow” (Matthew 13:3).
Close the Gospels; what could a hearer of Moses and the prophets make of that?
Start with the seed, which Isaiah had defined in one breath with the rain:

For as the rain cometh down… that it may give seed to the sower, and bread to the eater: so shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth…

The word is the seed to the sower and the bread to the eater — one verse, both figures.
And Moses had sung the same rain long before: “My doctrine shall drop as the rain, my speech shall distil as the dew” (Deuteronomy 32:2) — what falls from heaven to make the ground bear is teaching.

Next the ground.
Jeremiah had already preached this parable as a command: “Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns” — and his very next sentence names the soil: “take away the foreskins of your heart” (Jeremiah 4:3-4) — plowing and circumcising, one operation in two figures: remove the blocking flesh so the seed can enter.
Hosea gives the same order in the same words: “break up your fallow ground: for it is time to seek the LORD” (Hosea 10:12).
The ground is the heart, and the thorns were choking Judah's heart seven centuries before the sermon by the sea — and the thorns have a pedigree older still, for they are the curse-ground's own crop: “thorns also and thistles shall it (the ground) bring forth to thee” (Genesis 3:18), what the cursed earth grows where food should stand.

Now derive what the thorns mean, for the Old Testament assigns that too.
Read the sentence they grow in: the same curse that gives the ground its thorns sentences the man to anxious toil for his bread — “in sorrow shalt thou eat of it… in the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread” (Genesis 3:17, 19) — the thorns spring up in the field of the struggle for a living.
And that pair of weeds — thorn and thistle together — returns exactly once more in the Hebrew Scriptures, and Hosea builds the whole indictment around it:

Israel is an empty vine, he bringeth forth fruit unto himself: according to the multitude of his fruit he hath increased the altars; according to the goodness of his land they have made goodly images.
Their heart is divided; now shall they be found faulty…

The high places also of Aven, the sin of Israel, shall be destroyed: the thorn and the thistle shall come up on their altars; and they shall say to the mountains, Cover us; and to the hills, Fall on us.

Increase, a divided heart, and the curse-ground's own crop sprouting on the altars: riches choking the heart is Hosea's picture before it is the parable's.

Isaiah's vineyard tells the same story, and he graded it himself.
The vineyard planted with the choicest vine gave wild grapes instead, and the sentence fell:

And I will lay it waste: it shall not be pruned, nor digged; but there shall come up briers and thorns: I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it.

Isaiah then hands over the key:

For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant: and he looked for judgment, but behold oppression; for righteousness, but behold a cry.

The vineyard is Israel, and its briers and thorns are men — the woes that follow name them, person by person:

Woe unto them that join house to house, that lay field to field, till there be no place, that they may be placed alone in the midst of the earth!

Here is the monopoly-builder — buying house after house and field after field until no one else has a place, alone in the middle of everything he has swallowed.

Woe unto them that rise up early in the morning, that they may follow strong drink; that continue until night, till wine inflame them!
And the harp, and the viol, the tabret, and pipe, and wine, are in their feasts: but they regard not the work of the LORD, neither consider the operation of his hands.

Here is the pleasure-lover — feasting from morning drink to evening music, past all notice of God.
Riches and pleasures came up where fruit should have stood: Isaiah graded the thorns seven centuries before the sermon by the sea.

Even the stony ground was on record, for the heart God promises to replace is “the stony heart” (Ezekiel 36:26).
And why is the exchange a heart of flesh for a heart of stone?
Because flesh is ground: adam was formed “of the dust of the ground,” adamah (Genesis 2:7) — the man is named for the soil he is — and he was sent forth “to till the ground from whence he was taken” (Genesis 3:23), so the Sower's field was staked out in Eden.
No one plows rock — “will one plow there with oxen?” (Amos 6:12) — and the very oracle that promises the heart of flesh promises its plowing: “I am for you… and ye shall be tilled and sown” (Ezekiel 36:9).
The seed that found “no deepness of earth” on stone takes root in flesh: the law once carved on “tables of stone” written now “in fleshy tables of the heart” (2 Corinthians 3:3) — “ye are God's husbandry” (1 Corinthians 3:9).

What does ground bring forth when the seed takes?
Grass — “all flesh is grass” (Isaiah 40:6) — a symbol with a chapter of its own.

What of the fowls that devour the wayside seed?
The first time birds descend on a covenant in Scripture, they come as devourers: “when the fowls came down upon the carcases, Abram drove them away” (Genesis 15:11) — uninvited, snatching at the covenant sacrifice, driven off by the covenant man.
In Egypt, Joseph heard a dream of birds eating baked bread out of a basket and graded it without hesitation as a sentence of death (Genesis 40:17-19).
Birds that snatch what was given out of its place are the enemy's agents; a boy raised on Genesis could have written that down.

.The Teacher grades the derivation

|===
| Element | Derived from the Law and the Prophets | The Teacher's key

| Seed
| The word — rain-borne seed, rain-borne doctrine (Isa 55:10-11; Deut 32:2)
| “The seed is the word of God” (Luke 8:11)

| Ground
| The heart — plowed, circumcised, tilled and sown (Jer 4:3-4; Hos 10:12; Ezek 36:9, 26; Gen 2:7)
| The word “sown in his heart” (Matt 13:19)

| Fowls
| The devourers on the covenant and on the bread (Gen 15:11; 40:17-19)
| “Then cometh the wicked one, and catcheth away that which was sown” (Matt 13:19)

| Thorns
| The curse-crop; riches dividing the heart (Gen 3:17-19; Hos 10:1-8; Isa 5:6-12)
| “The care of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, choke the word” (Matt 13:22)
|===

Four for four — Isaiah's answer, Jeremiah's, Abram's, Hosea's — and not one of the four needed a word Jesus had not yet spoken.
His astonishment in Mark 4:13 was just.

Yet let me be fair, for I would have fared no better.
Handed the parable with no Bible in reach, I would have failed it as completely as any man on the shore.
With a Bible and a printed concordance — and the assurance that the answer was in there somewhere — the derivation above might have cost me days, or months.
It is only with modern tools that I can derive the interpretation independently at all, without leaning on any man's commentary.

Daniel was told to seal the words “even to the time of the end,” when “many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall be increased” (Daniel 12:4).
The running to and fro is through the scriptures themselves — and the knowledge increased is this.

SOURCE: books/symbolic-language/31-the-pearl.adoc

The kingdom of heaven is likened to a merchant man seeking goodly pearls, who finds one pearl of great price, sells all that he has, and buys it.
Jesus left this parable unkeyed — no interpretation is recorded — so the derivation stands where the Parables of the Kingdom chapter left it: on our method alone, tested like everything else and held fast if it proves good.

The method begins with the parable's own key words: a merchant; goodly — simply good; and one pearl — for one is no mere count.
Of all the goodly pearls the merchant finds, he sells everything for exactly one, and one signals what it signals everywhere in Scripture: complete, whole, undivided — a thing nothing can be added to.
Search those words through Scripture, and they gather at one address.

The pearls come first, and the King James buried them.
The Parables of the Kingdom chapter already dug them out from under the King James’ “rubies”: the Hebrew peninim is, by Strong's own definition, “probably a pearl (as round).”
Recovered, the pearls keep exactly the parable's company: Wisdom is priced above pearls (Proverbs 3:15; 8:11; Job 28:18) — and the seeker who searches for her “as for hid treasures” (Proverbs 2:4) is himself the merchant of the parable.
And the virtuous woman — the one bride — is “far above pearls” (Proverbs 31:10), drawn up out of the sea of the nations.

Now the merchant and his good.
Solomon prices wisdom in the merchant's own terms — “For the merchandise of it is better than the merchandise of silver” (Proverbs 3:14) — and Scripture stamps that merchandise good in exactly two more places in all its pages.
The first is the woman of this same book — “her merchandise is good” (Proverbs 31:18) — and in the Hebrew this is no echo but a quotation: letter for letter the clause of 3:14, כִּי־טוֹב סַחְרָהּ, “for her merchandise is good.”
The second is the parable itself: the kingdom's “merchant man, seeking goodly pearls” (Matthew 13:45).
Three texts, one thread — wisdom, the woman, the pearl: the good merchandise.

Proverbs interchanges the subject in its own grammar: the find-verb of 3:13 returns exactly twice in the book — “whoso findeth me” (8:35, Wisdom speaking) and “whoso findeth a wife” (18:22).
Wisdom and the bride hold one slot in Solomon's sentences, and the parable's pearl prices them both.
The merchant's vocabulary has led to two poems — wisdom's and the bride's — and this book reads poems like these on the bare letters.

What follows is each poem rendered afresh from the bare letters.
Where the plain King James reading is best, it stands untouched; every word changed is changed to an attested sense of the same letters, and every change is weighed, word by word, before this chapter ends.
Nothing here unseats the wife and mother of the plain reading — both readings run at once.
First, hear the poems clean.

Blessed is the man that findeth wisdom, and the man that draweth out understanding.
For the gain of her going-round is better than the going-round of silver, and her harvest than fine gold.
She is more bright than pearls: and all thy delights are not to be compared unto her.
Length and appropriateness of days is in her right hand; and in her left hand riches and shining.
Her ways are ways of splendour, and all her paths are wholeness.
She is a tree of life to them that lay hold upon her: and blessed is every one that holdeth her fast.
The LORD by wisdom hath founded the earth; by understanding hath he established the heavens.
By his knowledge the depths were broken open, and the skies drop down the dew.

A woman of valour who can find? for her price is far above pearls.
The heart of her husband doth safely trust in her, and gain shall never diminish.
She doeth him good and not evil all the days of her life.
She seeketh wool, and flax, and worketh willingly with her palms.
She is like the ships of the one who travels round; she bringeth her bread from afar.
She riseth also while it is yet night, and giveth the covenant's meat to her household, and the appointed portion to her maidens.
She considereth a field, and taketh it: with the fruit of her palms she planteth a vineyard.
She girdeth her loins with strength, and strengtheneth her arms.
She tasteth that it is good, her merchandise: her lamp goeth not out in the night.
She layeth her hands to the spindle, and her palms hold fast the circuit.
She spreadeth out her palm to the poor; yea, she reacheth forth her hands to the needy.
She is not worried by the whiteness for her household: for all her household are clothed in double.
She maketh herself coverings; her clothing is white linen and purple.
Her husband is known in the gates, when he sitteth among the elders of the land.
She maketh linen wraps, and selleth them; and delivereth girdles unto the merchant.
Strength and splendour are her clothing; and she laugheth at the last day.
She openeth her mouth with wisdom; and in her tongue is the law of kindness.
She keepeth the watch over the walkings of her household, and eateth not the bread of idleness.
Her sons arise, and call her blessed; her husband also, and he maketh her shine.
Many daughters have done valiantly, but thou hast gone up above them all.
Charm is a lie, and beauty a vapour: a woman that feareth the LORD, she it is that shall shine.
Give her of the fruit of her hands; and let her own works make her shine in the gates.

The Sun, Moon, and Stars chapter read the lights: the sun the Father and the husband; the moon the faithful witness — the Son toward His Father, the bride toward her Bridegroom; the stars the righteous, gathered into the twelve; the elders seated among the host; and the gates of the sky's tabernacle, through which the lights come and go.
Lay the poems against that sky, line by line, and every line finds its station.

“She riseth also while it is yet night… her lamp goeth not out in the night” (31:15, 18).
Of all the lights a reader has ever seen, exactly one rises as the dark falls and burns until morning: the full moon, which climbs the east gate at sunset and holds the sky the whole night through.
And what she serves her household is the calendar's own food — “the covenant's meat… the appointed portion”: the portion-word is choq, the “ordinances of the moon and of the stars” by night (Jeremiah 31:35).

“She is more bright than pearls” (3:15).
“Bright” is the King James’ own word for the moon — “the moon walking in brightness” (Job 31:26) — the comparison priced in the moon-verse's own vocabulary.

“Length and appropriateness of days is in her right hand; and in her left hand riches and shining” (3:16).
The month's own length — twenty-nine days or thirty — is declared at her fulness, and declared fitting: the appointed day, the day of meeting, meat given “in due season” (Matthew 24:45).
And Strong's reads the right-hand word as “locally, the south,” and the left-hand word as “properly dark (as enveloped)” — the north: days in her bright hand, shining even in her dark one.

“She worketh willingly with her palms… her palms hold fast the circuit… She spreadeth out her palm to the poor” (31:13, 19, 20).
The poem says palm — kaph — where it could have said hand, and keeps the two words distinct inside single verses.
And kaph is a shape before it is a limb: Strong's spends the word on every curved, hollow container — the palm, the sole, the pans of the tabernacle, the bowl of a spoon — a rounded vessel made to hold and to cover.
It is the palm God laid over Moses while the glory passed by (Exodus 33:22); and here it is the curved cup that receives the Bridegroom's light and holds fast the circuit, carrying it round the year — then opens toward the poor, the King's own signature: “He shall deliver the needy when he crieth; the poor also” (Psalm 72:12), in the very psalm where they fear Him “with the sun and before the face of the moon” through all revolutions of time (72:5, as the letters run).

“She considereth a field, and taketh it: with the fruit of her palms she planteth a vineyard. She girdeth her loins with strength” (31:16-17).
This is the Bridegroom's own record in parable: He planted the vineyard (Matthew 21:33) — and Isaiah names it, “the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isaiah 5:7) — and He bought the field for the treasure hidden in it, and “the field is the world” (Matthew 13:44, 38).
And she strengthens what she plants, where the counterfeit of the last chapter's plan “didst weaken the nations” (Isaiah 14:12) and wears out the saints (Daniel 7:25): one plants and strengthens, the other wears down.

“She tasteth that it is good, her merchandise” (31:18).
The words first spoken over light itself — “and God saw the light, that it was good” (Genesis 1:4) — tasted now over the good merchandise of the three texts.

“She is not worried by the whiteness for her household: for all her household are clothed in double… her clothing is white linen and purple” (31:21-22).
Her household are the stars, and they want for no light: they are clothed in double — the reading the oldest translations kept — and her own weave is shesh, white linen by definition.

“Her husband is known in the gates, when he sitteth among the elders of the land” (31:23) — “and let her own works make her shine in the gates” (31:31).
Her husband, the sun of this portrait, is known in the gates — the doors of his own circuit through the twelve — and he sits among the elders, the bench the Sun, Moon, and Stars chapter seated among the host of heaven.
Her works shine at the same doors: the gates her fulness passes through, each one, the city says, a single pearl.

“Her sons arise, and call her blessed; her husband also, and he maketh her shine” (31:28).
The verb is halal, whose first sense is to shine: he makes her shine, as the sun makes the moon.

“Strength and splendour are her clothing; and she laugheth at the last day” (31:25).
Beneath the laugh, in the same letters, stands the shachaq — the sky where the faithful witness is established (Psalm 89:37) — and she can laugh at the day because she knows its date: Wisdom laughs at calamity (Proverbs 1:26) for the reason the psalm gives, “he seeth that his day is coming” (Psalm 37:13).

“She openeth her mouth with wisdom; and in her tongue is the law of kindness” (31:26).
That is the nightly speech of the nineteenth Psalm — “no speech nor language, where their voice is not heard”: the witness declares, and what she declares is torah, kindly.

Through all of it the poem never says moon; the Hebrew of the portrait contains no moon-word at all.
It paints a light that rises in the dark, shines the whole night with a shining her husband gives her, deals the appointed portions, holds the circuit — and withholds the name to the last line.
The Song of Songs supplies what the portrait withheld, singing the same two praise-verbs over the same one-above-the-daughters woman:

My dove, my undefiled is but one; she is the only one of her mother, she is the choice one of her that bare her.
The daughters saw her, and blessed her; yea, the queens and the concubines, and they praised her.
Who is she that looketh forth as the morning, fair as the moon, clear as the sun, and terrible as an army with banners?

The poem paints the portrait; the Song signs it.

Wisdom's poem reads the same way, line by line.
“She is a tree of life to them that lay hold upon her: and blessed is every one that holdeth her fast” (3:18) — the holding-verb is tamak, the verb of the palms holding the circuit, and the verb of Moses’ hands on the mountain, held up steady — emunah, the faithful-witness word — “until the going down of the sun,” while Joshua weakened Amalek — chalash, the rare verb of Isaiah 14:12, three occurrences in all of Scripture (Exodus 17:12-13).

“The LORD by wisdom hath founded the earth; by understanding hath he established the heavens” (3:19) — “established” is konen, the verb of “the moon and the stars, which thou hast ordained” (Psalm 8:3); the wisdom priced above pearls is the wisdom that built the sky — “when he prepared the heavens, I was there” (Proverbs 8:27).
“By his knowledge the depths were broken open, and the skies drop down the dew” (3:20) — the broken-open deeps are Genesis 7:11's, the flood's calendar-stamped ledger; and the “skies” are the shachaqim, the witness's own sky, dropping down the dew.

Mark the pearl's properties as Scripture handles the figure.
It is one: the merchant found “one pearl of great price” and stopped collecting, for the kingdom is not a collection but one bride, bought whole.
It is round and complete: the roundness sits inside Strong's definition itself.
It is white — a bearer of soft, borrowed light out of darkness — and it is born of the waters.
Then Revelation prices the city's entrances in it:

And the twelve gates were twelve pearls; every several gate was of one pearl…

The Greek doubles the point — each one of the gates, of one pearl — and the Hebrew Revelation doubles it the same way: every single gate, of one pearl.
Not gates studded with pearls: each gate is one pearl — one, complete, whole.
So the pearl, wherever Scripture spends it, is the one complete thing of great price — and it is a gate.
Now ask the merchant's question: has the King hung such a thing anywhere in plain sight — one, round, white, complete, and standing at a door?

Look up.
Of all the moon's phases and all the lights of heaven, exactly one is white, round, and complete: the night sky owns precisely one pearl.
And Scripture had already assigned that light its office: the moon appointed for the moedim, the appointed times, from the fourth day (Psalm 104:19; Genesis 1:14).

The pairing was set at the pattern's founding: Joseph's dream read the moon as the mother (Genesis 37:9-10), and the sun comes out of his chamber “as a bridegroom” (Psalm 19:5) — a bridegroom's answering light is his bride, the counterpart the Sun, Moon, and Stars chapter already seated facing him, moon toward her Bridegroom as the Son is moon toward His Father.

If the pearl has led truly, the letters should be waiting at the same spot — and they are.
Scripture keeps a “fulness” overhead, and the King James buried it exactly as it buried the pearls.
The Hebrew is keseh — Strong's: “properly, fulness or the full moon” — and most translations render it as what it is:

Blow the trumpet at the time of the New Moon, at the full moon, on our solemn feast day.

Here the King James stands nearly alone with its “in the time appointed”; the NKJV, the ESV, the NASB, the Jewish Publication Society's version — “at the full moon for our feast-day” — and Smith's Literal Translation all read full moon.
And the oldest translation of all leans the same way: the Septuagint, made centuries before Messiah, renders the day “in the glorious day of your feast” — the Greek is eusēmos, well-marked, conspicuous, built on sēma, a sign, the very root the Greek of Genesis 1:14 hangs the lights on, “for signs.”
Whatever else those translators heard in keseh, they heard the day the sky cannot hide — and of the moon's phases exactly one is conspicuous, while the dark conjunction is the one day the sky shows no sign at all.

The verse does not say “and” between the new moon and the full moon — one day, not two.
Some translations insert an “and” to split them apart; the Hebrew, rendered literally, in its own order, runs the other way — you shall blow with the new-moon trumpet in the full moon for the day of our festival sacrifice — the full moon is the head of the month, the feast-day of Numbers 10:10 and 28:11.

Solomon uses the same word for the day the traveling husband returns: “he will come home at the full moon” (Proverbs 7:20) — keseh again — and there it is spelled כסא, letter for letter the spelling of kisse’, “throne.”
The last chapter stood on that identity from the enemy's side; here is the LORD's side of it. Both words grow from one root, kasah, to cover, to fill — the throne is the covered seat, the full moon the filled light — and Job holds the two senses up in a single verse: “He holdeth back the face of his throne, and spreadeth his cloud upon it” (Job 26:9), the veiled face of His full moon.

If it is asked which way the covering runs — whether the throne-word is covered in darkness or covered in light — Scripture describes the throne itself.
Daniel saw the throne-room itself, and every detail belongs to this chapter:

I beheld till the thrones were set in place, and the Ancient of days did sit, whose garment was white as snow, and the hair of his head like the pure wool: his throne was like the fiery flame, and his wheels as burning fire.

The thrones are set — placed like lights in their stations. [Footnote: The King James prints “the thrones were cast down”; the Aramaic verb is one of placing, and the newer translations read it so — the thrones were set, not overthrown.]
And the title under “Ancient of days” is built on a root of moving onward, going before — read once, He is the Ancient of Days; read again, He is the Foremost of Days: the One at the head of the days, seated where the days begin.
His garment white as snow, His hair like the pure wool, His throne flame, His wheels burning fire — and the plural on “wheels” is the ending this book met on Daniel's sevens: an intensive, not a count — the wheel complete, the perfect circle of fire.

Whiteness enthroned on light; brightness round about it, “as the appearance of the bow that is in the cloud in the day of rain” (Ezekiel 1:26-28); and its Occupant “coverest thyself with light as with a garment” (Psalm 104:2).
If the throne is the keseh, Daniel's vision draws what the letters spell: the full moons set in their stations, and the Head of Days taking His seat — white, complete, covered in light — where the month begins.

The psalm that gave this book the faithful witness already sets the throne as the sun and as the moon — Psalm 89:36-37 — plain simile, not wordplay, and the throne is a throne of light. [Footnote: Derived in the Sun, Moon, and Stars chapter.]
Where darkness stands near it, it stands outside, as a veil: “clouds and darkness are round about him” (Psalm 97:2) — round about, not within — the cloud of Job 26:9 spread upon the face, holding the light back.
The keseh is covered in light; only the counterfeit is covered in dark.

The sky is built like a sanctuary — the tabernacle Psalm 19 pitched for the sun — and its front, like the tabernacle's, faces the sunrise, the east.
Now hear Ezekiel on the gates of the house:

Thus saith the Lord GOD; The gate of the inner court that looketh toward the east shall be shut the six working days; but on the sabbath it shall be opened, and in the day of the new moon it shall be opened.

Three kinds of days — working days, sabbaths, new-moon days (Amos knew the third kind too: “When will the new moon be gone, that we may sell corn?” Amos 8:5) — and on the day that begins the month, the east gate stands open.
A gate is opened because something is meant to come through it.
And exactly one phase enters by the east gate at the fall of night: the full moon enters in the east at the hour the portrait already fixed — through the front door of the sky's tabernacle, the faithful witness at maximum.

The sliver, by contrast, is hunted low in the west, at sunset, beside the sun — and the sheepfold has a rule about entrances:

Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that entereth not by the door into the sheepfold, but climbeth up some other way, the same is a thief and a robber.
But he that entereth in by the door is the shepherd of the sheep.

The prince of Ezekiel's house comes and goes “by the way of the gate that looketh toward the east” (Ezekiel 46:12).
The true light enters at the front gate; the counterfeit climbs in from the dark side — which is precisely the address his heart chose in the last chapter.

Now set the pieces together.
The pearl is the full moon; the city's pearl-gates are His appointed times — for the moedim are, as the last chapter read the word, meetings: the fixed days on which the King receives.
Twelve gates; twelve months of full moons; the stars of God gathered into the twelve constellations, the “Mazzaroth” brought forth “in his season” (Job 38:32), through which the full moon makes its yearly round.
And there Solomon's woman collects what her portrait promised — praised in the gates her fulness passes through, her husband at home among the elders.

The merchant who sold all he had for one pearl of great price was not buying jewelry.
He was buying his entry at the King's gate — the appointed time of meeting — and Isaiah had already welded the paired parables into one sentence: “wisdom and knowledge shall be the stability of thy times… the fear of the LORD is his treasure” (Isaiah 33:6).
The treasure and the times; the pearl and the gate.

“It is the glory of God to conceal a thing: but the honour of kings is to search out a matter” (Proverbs 25:2) — He hid the pearl where only a merchant who would sell everything looks.

Jesus spent the pearl-word one other time, and it is a warning:

Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you.

The dogs and the swine are one family — unclean beasts, the nations outside the covenant table.
And what swine do to pearls is exactly what Scripture says the nations do to holy things: they tread them underfoot — “it is given unto the Gentiles: and the holy city shall they tread under foot” (Revelation 11:2); the sanctuary and the host “trodden under foot” (Daniel 8:13); “Jerusalem shall be trodden down of the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles be fulfilled” (Luke 21:24).

Mark the last word of that sentence: what the trampling runs until is a matter of times.
If the pearl is the appointed time of meeting, the warning reads whole: hand the holy times to the nations and they will not keep them — they will trample them, and turn and rend the hand that gave them.
Daniel named the plan — to change the times and the laws; this verse is the Lord's advance notice of how the theft would look on the ground — the pearl underfoot.

Read this chapter and the last as the pair they are.
The enemy raises the moon covered in darkness; the LORD's sign is the same seat covered in light — the Father's whole face borne through the dark.
One moon reflects everything; the other reflects nothing, for its source produces only dark.
One enters by the door; the other climbs up some other way.

The sky itself stages the ambition, for the two moons stand in two different places: the full moon, standing always opposite, can never come between; only the moon covered in darkness can stand over the sun — slide before his face and put out the day at noon — and blot the stars from the same sky.
That is the plan of the last chapter drawn in one picture — “Woe unto them… that put darkness for light, and light for darkness” (Isaiah 5:20).

The stars — the righteous, who keep time — follow one moon or the other.
That is why the parable's merchant sells all: the pearl is not an ornament on the kingdom; it is the gate into it, and there has only ever been one seller who could ask that price and one buyer who paid it gladly.

Grade this chapter the way the Parables of the Kingdom chapter graded everything, for the method matters more than any single finding.
Every link stands in the text: the pearl-word under the King James’ “rubies”; the city's gates each of one pearl; the moon set over the moedim from the fourth day; the fulness-word under “throne” and “time appointed” confirming where the pearl had already led; the east gate opened on the new-moon day; and the two poems rendered whole on the bare letters, every departure weighed word by word.
The chain that joins the links is a reading — this book's reading, offered to be tested, not swallowed.

The reckoning that follows from it — where the month truly begins, how the sabbaths fall, what history did to the calendar and what the sky and the records of the nations still testify — is a book of its own. [Footnote: The complete case is made in Time Tested Tradition: The Renewed Biblical Calendar.]
This chapter needs only the symbol.
The kingdom has a gate; the gate is one complete pearl; and the merchant who understands what is being sold does not haggle.

The rule of the What Is the Point? chapter cuts both ways: the pointing gets a vote, not a veto — and neither does the re-reading, until the letters and the witnesses agree.
Here, then, is every departure, weighed; whatever is not listed is the King James untouched.

In wisdom's poem (Proverbs 3:13-20):

- draweth out (3:13) — puq, Strong's “to issue, draw out”; the King James’ “getteth” flattens a verb of drawing forth.
- going-round (3:14) — sachar, “to travel round (as a pedlar); traffic” — the merchant-word of 31:14, 18; rendered by its own root-sense.
- harvest (3:14) — tevuah, “income, i.e. produce”; the King James renders it “increase” and “fruits” elsewhere — the field-word, kept agricultural.
- bright (3:15) — yaqar: the King James’ own rendering at Job 31:26 — “the moon walking in brightness” — the one place it describes a light.
- pearls (3:15; 31:10) — peninim, Strong's “probably a pearl (as round)”; the chapter's founding recovery.
- length and appropriateness of days / shining (3:16) — the root under orek keeps a second sense in the same letters: arik, “it was not meet for us” (Ezra 4:14), Strong's “reaching to a given point; to suit” — the days counted and fitted; and kavod is glory as Scripture displays it, radiance — “Arise, shine; for thy light is come, and the glory of the LORD is risen upon thee” (Isaiah 60:1).
- splendour / wholeness (3:17) — noam, “agreeableness, i.e. delight, suitableness, splendor”; shalom, “safe, i.e. well, happy... completeness” — peace as the whole and unbroken.
- holdeth her fast (3:18) — tamak, “to sustain; to obtain, keep fast” — the verb of 31:19.
- established (3:19) — konen (H3559), the verb of Psalm 8:3, “the moon and the stars, which thou hast ordained.”
- broken open / skies (3:20) — baqa, the verb of Genesis 7:11 (“were all the fountains of the great deep broken up”); shachaqim, the sky-word of Psalm 89:37.

In the bride's portrait (Proverbs 31:10-31):

- never diminish (31:11) — chaser: Strong's King James column reads “decrease, abated, fail” — the gain that does not wane.
- palms (31:13, 16, 19, 20) — kaph, “the hollow hand or palm,” kept visible because the poem itself sets kaph beside yad inside single verses (vv19-20): the palm and the hand are distinguished by the poet, not by us.
- the one who travels round (31:14) — sachar again, the same going-round as 3:14.
- taketh it (31:16) — the written verb is laqach, to take; the King James prints “buyeth it.”
- the covenant's meat / the appointed portion (31:15) — teref is the noun of Psalm 111:5, “he hath given meat unto them that fear him: he will ever be mindful of his covenant”; choq is “an enactment; an appointment (of time)” — the King James’ own “set time” (Job 14:13), and the word of Jeremiah 31:35's moon-and-stars ordinances.
- tasteth that it is good / in the night (31:18) — the Hebrew order restored: טָעֲמָה כִּי־טוֹב — “she tasteth that it is good,” the ki tov spoken over the light (Genesis 1:4); “in the night” is the written text (the kethib).
- the circuit (31:19) — pelekh, “from an unused root meaning to be round; a circuit... also a spindle (as whirled)”; the King James itself renders it as a district (“part,” Nehemiah 3). Both spin: the housewife's whorl and the sky's round.
- not worried by the whiteness / in double (31:21) — yare is fear in the sense of anxious care, and sheleg, snow, is Scripture's standard of whiteness (“white as snow,” Isaiah 1:18); and the letters שנים read as shnayim, “double”: so the Septuagint (“garments of double texture”), the Vulgate, and Smith's Literal Translation; the pointing reads shanim, “scarlet.” The elder witnesses carry the double; the same letters also spell “years” — a revolution of time.
- white linen (31:22) — shesh, “bleached stuff, i.e. white linen” — the whiteness sits inside the plain word; the King James’ “silk” is the departure, not ours.
- laugheth at the last day (31:25) — sachaq + le-yom acharon: so Young's Literal (“she rejoiceth at a latter day”), the Douay-Rheims (“she shall laugh in the latter day”), and Smith's Literal; the identical phrase is “the last day” at Isaiah 30:8. And unpointed, שחק is also shachaq — the witness's sky — a second reading standing in the letters.
- keepeth the watch / walkings (31:27) — tsofiyah, the watchman's verb (“I have made thee a watchman,” Ezekiel 3:17); halichot, “a walking, a procession” — the family of Job 31:26's moon “walking in brightness.”
- maketh her shine / she it is that shall shine / make her shine in the gates (31:28, 30, 31) — halal, whose base sense is “to shine” before it is “to praise” (the King James’ own “when his candle shined,” Job 29:3; “the moon walking in brightness” verse sits in the same field): to praise her is to make her shine, and both senses are true at once.
- gone up above them all (31:29) — alah, “thou hast gone up”: so Young's and Smith's, literally.
- vapour (31:30) — hevel, “breath, vapour” — Ecclesiastes’ word, rendered literally.

Weigh them all; the reading asks no favors.
Every changed word is an attested sense of the very letters the scribes counted, most of them the King James’ own renderings from other verses — and the elder witnesses, the Greek and the Latin, already read the doubled garments a thousand years before the points were fixed.
The pointing keeps the housewife; the letters keep the housewife and the light she was always painted from.
Both are true — that is how this language testifies.

The appointed times the pearl governs are counted in sevens — and the word Scripture counts them with is the next chapter.
